claims.text: The relevant Mg-containing lightweight high-entropy alloy has a density below 6 g/cm3.
The as-cast alloy is a homogeneous, single-phase, non-equilibrium solid solution with uniformly distributed Mg.
Controlled thermal or environmental exposure induces Mg diffusion in the non-equilibrium alloy.
Mg diffusion transforms the homogeneous metastable solid solution into a microstructure containing Mg-rich intermetallic precipitates.
Formation of Mg-rich precipitates leaves a complementary matrix enriched in passivating elements such as Ti, Zn, or Al.
The evolved microstructure forms a denser and more adherent composite oxide scale during high-temperature oxidation.
Microstructural evolution modifies the local electrochemical contrasts controlling corrosion.
The evolved oxide scale improves high-temperature oxidation resistance relative to the as-cast state.
The microstructural evolution alters corrosion kinetics relative to the as-cast state.
A controlled anneal at 700–900 °C can be used to induce the proposed evolution.
Exposure conditions can permit slow diffusion-driven evolution without fully equilibrating the alloy.
The interfacial composite oxide may comprise TiO2, ZnO, or Al2O3.
Mg is highly mobile in the non-equilibrium microstructure.
Mg depletion from the matrix and segregation into intermetallic compounds redistribute other reactive elements.
Enrichment of the matrix in passivating elements enhances nucleation and growth of a protective oxide at high temperature.
The changed phase dispersion reduces microgalvanic couples affecting corrosion reactions.
The thermally evolved alloy will exhibit lower oxidation mass gain or slower oxidation kinetics than the as-cast alloy.
The thermally evolved alloy will exhibit a measurable change, potentially a decrease, in corrosion current density relative to the as-cast alloy.
The proposed mechanism applies up to approximately 900 °C and in typical chloride-containing environments.
The comparison uses an as-cast control and an otherwise identical alloy annealed at 800 °C for 100 hours.
